title: AdaniConneX Google Vizag Data Centres Will Use Air Cooling, Slashing Freshwater Use
excerpt: Project details for the roughly 1-gigawatt Visakhapatnam campuses, developed with Google, cap freshwater use across three sites at less than an Olympic pool and rule out municipal supply lines.
body:
• AdaniConneX's Visakhapatnam data centre campuses, developed in partnership with Google, will use air-cooled systems instead of water-based evaporative cooling, according to project details reported by PTI.
  • Freshwater use across the three sites is planned to stay below the volume of an Olympic-sized swimming pool, with about 80 percent of that water going to landscaping, kitchens and worker facilities and then recycled on site.
  • The campuses at Mudasarlova and Tarluvada form part of a proposed development of about 1 gigawatt, near the Mudasarlova Reservoir and the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary.
  • For readers tracking India's AI build-out: the design answers the project's sharpest local criticism — that a gigawatt of computing would compete with households for drinking water — by using dedicated industrial connections rather than municipal supplies.

AdaniConneX's planned data centre campuses in Visakhapatnam, being developed in partnership with Google, will use air-cooled systems to eliminate the need for water-based evaporative cooling, according to project details reported by The Hindu BusinessLine and NDTV. Freshwater consumption across the three sites is planned to remain at less than the volume of an Olympic-sized swimming pool.

The campuses at Mudasarlova and Tarluvada are part of a proposed data centre development with a capacity of about 1 gigawatt, as Visakhapatnam seeks to emerge as a major hub for artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. AdaniConneX is a joint venture between Adani Enterprises and US-based EdgeConneX, developing a nationwide network of hyperscale data centres for cloud computing, artificial intelligence and digital services.

How the Water Plan Works

Unlike conventional data centres that use evaporative cooling systems and cooling towers, the proposed facilities will rely on air-based cooling technology, avoiding the large volumes of water typically consumed by such systems, sources with knowledge of the matter said. Cooling is normally a data centre's main source of water demand.

Of the limited freshwater required across the three sites, around 80 percent will be used for landscaping, kitchens and worker facilities, with water recycled and reused on site, the sources said. The facilities will have dedicated industrial water connections rather than draw supplies from municipal lines, a move aimed at preventing competition with households for drinking water.

The project will also follow a zero-discharge policy for domestic wastewater. That wastewater will be treated at an on-site sewage treatment plant and reused for landscape irrigation and flushing, and no treated wastewater will be discharged into the Mudasarlova Reservoir, according to the project details.

Why Water Became the Central Argument

The measures are intended to reduce the campuses' impact on local water resources, including the Mudasarlova Reservoir, a source of drinking water for the city, and the adjoining Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary. Water consumption has emerged as a key concern in the debate over Andhra Pradesh's push to attract large data centre investments, because the facilities require substantial cooling capacity to support energy-intensive computing and artificial intelligence workloads.

The controversy intensified after Andhra Pradesh approved Google's proposed AI data centre hub in Visakhapatnam, being developed with AdaniConneX, with environmental activists questioning its proximity to the reservoir and the sanctuary. Critics have also raised concerns over the adequacy of environmental assessments and the disclosure of operational water requirements. The state government has defended the project, with IT Minister Nara Lokesh dismissing claims about its resource needs as misinformation. The government has said the proposed data centre ecosystem, if expanded to 6.5 gigawatts, could require around 3 TMC of water annually, while Google has said it plans to use advanced air-cooling technology.

"Nations that master the symmetry between energy and compute will shape the next decade. India is uniquely positioned to lead."

— Gautam Adani, Chairman, Adani Group

A Wider Data Centre Race in Vizag

Visakhapatnam is attracting investments in data centres and supporting digital infrastructure as companies expand capacity to meet rising demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence services. Reliance Industries is also developing a data centre campus near Bhogapuram and Polipalli, while Bharti Airtel is investing in terrestrial and metropolitan fibre networks and undersea cable landing infrastructure at Rambilli.

The Vizag campus also anchors a much larger group roadmap. Adani has announced plans to take its data centre target to 5 gigawatts, building on AdaniConneX's existing 2-gigawatt portfolio and pipeline, in an expansion announced by the group alongside partnerships with Google in Visakhapatnam and Microsoft in Hyderabad and Pune.

What to Watch

The air-cooling commitment shifts the project's main resource question from water to electricity: air-based systems avoid evaporative water loss but still have to move the same heat, so the campuses' power sourcing will draw scrutiny as construction proceeds. For now, the developers' position is specific and testable — freshwater use below one Olympic pool across three sites, no municipal supply lines, and no treated wastewater reaching the reservoir that supplies the city's drinking water.
